en: The Śivanakṣatramālikā Stotra Śrīkaṇṭha,
Sāmba, Īśāna, the beloved life-breath of Pārvatī,
mounted upon the bull, the friend of Viṣṇu— Śiva alone is my refuge. 1
The Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, the five-faced Supreme Lord,
the abode higher than the highest— Śiva alone is my refuge.
He is without support, formless, stainless, and free from affliction.
Śiva alone, who is eternally pure and stainless, is my refuge.
(3) Resembling pure crystal, with the sun, moon, and fire as his eyes, bearing the trident and the axe—Śarva, Śiva alone, is my refuge. (4)
He who has the earth as his chariot, Viṣṇu as his arrow, the Vedas as his horses, and Brahmā as his charioteer;
the enemy of Tripura, whose bow is Mount Meru—Śiva alone is my refuge.
Clad in a tiger-skin garment and wearing a serpent as his sacred thread;
Śiva alone, who eternally bestows all desired objects, is my refuge.
(6) The great Time, the Time of time, whose body is smeared with ashes, Śambhu whose abode is Kailāsa—He alone is my refuge. (7)
Adorned with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, his forehead marked with the triple line (tripuṇḍra),
the Lord of the Pramathas, Mahādeva— Śiva alone is my refuge.
Gaurī’s beloved, Vāmadeva, blue-throated and clad in the directions as his garment.
Gaṅgādhara, Candracūḍa, Śiva alone is my refuge.
(9) Rich in the nature of the three forms, yet devoid of the three qualities, and the ordainer of the three tasks—Śiva alone is my refuge. (10)
Sadyojāta, Bhairava, the granter of boons to Mārkaṇḍeya,
and the giver of Viṣṇu’s discus— Śiva alone is my refuge.
Aghora-mūrti, the Lord of all, known through the Vedas, the ocean of compassion.
Śiva alone, whose lotus-hand is joined with a skull, is my refuge.
Śiva alone—the eight-formed Tatpuruṣa, likewise the eleven-formed, and the twenty-five-fold playful soul—is my refuge. (12–13)
Richly endowed with the nature of the hundred Rudras, the bestower of boons upon Nandi and Bhṛṅgi,
Sadāśiva of infinite forms— Śiva alone is my refuge.
Born from the Great Liṅga, peaceful, adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Triyambaka, Virūpākṣa, Śiva alone is my refuge.
(15) The stainless one, the supreme light, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, Śiva—who is enriched by the form of the hunter Māyā—is my refuge alone. (16)
In the form of a *liṅga*, ten-armed, fierce, Paśupati, Bhava,
Kāmeśvara, the protector of the world— Śiva alone is my refuge.
(17) He whose form is auspicious and beautiful, the bestower of boons for desired objects.
Śiva alone, who is ever-distracted by the playful dance of Hālāsya, is my refuge.
(18) Mṛtyuñjaya, Mahāraudra, Soma, Skanda, Maheśvara, and the protector of Bāṇāsura—Śiva alone is my refuge. (19)
The severer of Jalandhara’s head, adorned with serpent ornaments,
wearing an elephant hide as a garment— Śiva alone is my refuge.
He is the remover of the disease of worldly existence, the worshipful one, the creator of fear and the destroyer of fear.
Śiva alone, rich in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, is my refuge.
(21) Hara, the dancer at twilight, Rudra, the granter of boons to the Asuras, the wielder of the Pināka bow, and the enemy of Manmatha—Śiva alone is my refuge. (22)
The compassionate one, the severer of Brahmā’s head, the bestower of boons upon Vināyaka,
the Lord Umāmaheśvara— Śiva alone is my refuge.
He is the Great Lord, the Great Yogin, surrounded by a multitude of beings.
Śiva alone, who is praised by sages such as Nārada, is my refuge.
(24) The hero who destroyed Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the consumer of ten million units of poison, the progenitor and teacher of Gaṇeśa—Śiva alone is my refuge. (25)
Kuberamitra, Bhīmeśa, Girīśa, and the beloved of Mohinī;
served by gods, asuras, and others—Śiva alone is my refuge.
Sthāṇu, whose self is both Hari and Hara, and the giver of the Tāraka mantra to Rāma.
Śaṅkara, who is Śiva himself as Ardhanārīśa, is my sole refuge.
O Śrī Cāmuṇḍā, filled with compassion, [I am] devoted to the meditation on Śiva;
Śrī Kṛṣṇendra, endowed with devotion, [offers] this garland of Śiva’s constellations.
Having composed it, he offered it into the lotus-heart of Śrīkaṇṭha.
Whoever recites this with devotion at the three junctions of the day shall attain union with Śiva.

In the year [measured by] the gems, mountains, and lords of the earth (1779), on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Siddha (Phālguna), on a Monday, this flower-garland named *Gajabhānu*—resplendent as gold, consisting of fifty syllables, and dedicated at the feet of the moon-crested Lord (Śiva) by King Kṛṣṇa—is completed.
Thus ends the *Śrīśivanakṣatramālikāstotra*.
